title: Ibn Gabirol
hook: poet and philosopher; his poem Keter Malchut is read on Yom Kippur night

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samuel HaNagid. Your line was poet and statesman. Today, a poet with only a pen.

Yom Kippur night. The long evening service is over, the synagogue half empty, the lights low. In some communities a few people stay on, open a prayer book to a long poem, and read it slowly, aloud or under their breath. It starts at the edge of the universe and ends with one person admitting how small they are. The poem is Keter Malchut, the royal crown. Its author was a poet in Spain who, by his own poems' account, was often lonely, sick, and at odds with the people around him, and who wrote as if the whole sky were his to describe. Today, Solomon ibn Gabirol.
screen: `YOM KIPPUR NIGHT, LIGHTS LOW.` → `A LONG POEM, READ SLOWLY.` → `KETER MALCHUT: THE ROYAL CROWN.`

segments.voice: Keter Malchut moves in three wide steps. First, it praises God with a string of names and attributes: God is one, God lives, God is great, God is light. Then it tours the universe as his time pictured it: earth, waters, moon, planets, stars, sphere beyond sphere, each a sign of its maker. And then, after all that size, it turns. The speaker looks at himself: a body made of dust, a short life, a list of wrongs. He confesses and asks for mercy. That turn is the heart of it. The bigger the sky gets, the more honest the person under it has to be, which is why it fits Yom Kippur, the day of atonement. The poem leans on a much older song. Psalm one hundred four, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, says: "O LORD my God, Thou art very great; Thou art clothed with glory and majesty. Who coverest Thyself with light as with a garment." Ibn Gabirol takes that psalm's habit of looking at creation and praising, and stretches it across the whole sky. He wrote other things too: philosophy about how the world comes from God, and personal poems about friendship, loneliness and grief. Some of his religious poems found their way into the prayer books of different communities. Keep the title's image: the poet weaves a crown out of words, offers it up, then stands bareheaded and tells the truth about himself.
screen: `PRAISE: GOD IS ONE, GOD IS LIGHT.` · `A TOUR OF THE WHOLE SKY.` · `THE TURN: AN HONEST CONFESSION.` · then, large: `LIGHT AS WITH A GARMENT.`

segments.voice: Take the line from Psalm one hundred four, light as with a garment, or any short poem you love, and say the first line in your head, then pause. Let one image stay, and notice what it does to your breathing before you go on, just as slowly. If you pray, you can let the words of the psalm be your prayer.
Ibn Gabirol. Solomon ibn Gabirol, poet and philosopher of Spain, whose long poem Keter Malchut moves from the whole sky to an honest confession. Today's word.
Your line: the royal crown. Praise first, then the honest look at yourself. That's day nine hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: In some communities Keter Malchut is read privately or aloud on the night of Yom Kippur after the evening service, and several of Ibn Gabirol's poems appear in Jewish prayer books.
